content: In the United States, a Level I trauma center represents the highest standard of surgical care available for trauma patients. These centers are mandated to have a specific number of surgeons and anesthesiologists physically present and available at the hospital 24 hours a day. Additionally, they must maintain educational programs, as well as preventive and community outreach initiatives. Key features of a Level I trauma center include round-the-clock, in-house availability of general surgeons. In most states across the U.S., hospitals designated as Level I trauma centers are accredited by the American College of Surgeons (ACS) for a three-year period. However, some states, such as Pennsylvania, New York, and Florida, have their own systems for ranking trauma centers. For example, Pennsylvania uses criteria established by the Commonwealth's Trauma Foundation. It is important to note that the ACS does not officially designate hospitals as regional trauma centers. Despite this, many hospitals that are not listed on the ACS trauma roster still refer to their emergency or trauma units as Level I trauma centers. The ACS describes the process of trauma center designation as a geopolitical process in which authorized entities, whether governmental or otherwise, are empowered to assign such designations. The ACS’s role is limited to verifying and reporting whether a hospital meets the standards outlined in its guidelines, known as Resources for Optimal Care of the Injured Patient. Trauma care is also provided at lower levels, which include Level II, Level III, and Level IV trauma centers, each offering progressively less comprehensive services.
